The Three Pillars of AI Monitoring

sections.title: Introduction
sections.body: > **Prerequisite**: File 08 (tracing). You can capture spans, build a trace tree, and reconstruct why a request behaved the way it did. This file turns tracing *on for the whole fleet*: how to watch the system after deployment, detect silent failures, alert before users notice, and feed everything back into evaluation. File 10 (continuous evaluation) consumes the signals we collect here.

sections.title: 1. Why Monitoring AI ≠ Monitoring Traditional Software
sections.body:
Traditional software monitoring has been solved for two decades. You watch four signals: **uptime**, **error rate**, **latency**, and **resource utilization** (CPU, memory, disk). If those are green, the system is healthy. The contract is binary: a request either returns the correct response or it doesn't. A 500 error is unambiguous.

AI breaks this contract. An LLM call returns `200 OK` with a perfectly formatted, grammatically fluent, completely wrong answer. A RAG system retrieves five chunks, all valid, none relevant. An agent executes its tool calls in the wrong order and still reports "task complete." From the load balancer's perspective, every one of these requests *succeeded*. From the user's perspective, they failed catastrophically. This is the **silent failure** problem: the system looks healthy by every traditional metric while quietly eroding user trust.

AI monitoring therefore extends the traditional four signals with a second tier:

| Signal type | Traditional software | AI system |
|---|---|---|
| Availability | Uptime, error rate | + Model refusal rate, safety-block rate |
| Performance | Latency p50/p95/p99 | + Tokens/sec, time-to-first-token, queue depth |
| Correctness | Implicit (200 = correct) | Explicit: faithfulness, groundedness, hallucination rate |
| Stability | Deployment version drift | + **Data drift**, **concept drift**, **prediction drift** |
| Cost | Server hours | + Token cost, per-model spend, prompt-cache hit rate |
| Regression | Code diff | + Model swap, prompt version, retrieval index version |
| User signal | Crash reports | + Thumbs up/down, regenerate clicks, dwell time |
| Failure mode | Crash, 500 | Hallucination, refusal, off-topic, stale embedding |

The right half of this table is the entire reason this file exists. A team that ships an LLM app and instruments only the left half will not notice when their faithfulness drops 15% over a week — because nothing on the left half will move.

sections.title: 2. The Three Pillars of AI Monitoring
sections.body:
Production AI monitoring rests on three pillars. Each answers a different question, uses different tools, and fails differently when neglected.

```
                  Production AI Monitoring
                            |
          +-----------------+-----------------+
          |                 |                 |
   1. QUALITY        2. OPERATIONAL     3. COST
   "Is output        "Is system         "Are we
    still good?"      healthy?"          bleeding money?"
   |                 |                 |
   - faithfulness    - latency p50/95/99  - cost / req
   - hallucination   - tokens/sec         - cost / task success
   - groundedness    - error rate         - token efficiency
   - drift (PSI/JS)  - cache hit rate     - model mix
   - LLM-judge       - queue depth        - budget burn rate
   - user feedback   - tool failure rate  - anomaly on spend
   |                 |                 |
   fails silently   fails loudly      fails expensively
```

**Quality monitoring** asks whether the output is still correct. It is the hardest pillar because correctness is not directly observable in production — you rarely have ground truth. You infer it from samples, judges, user feedback, and drift signals. It fails *silently*: nothing alerts, users slowly churn.

**Operational monitoring** asks whether the system is healthy. This is closest to traditional monitoring: latency, throughput, error rate, cache hit rate. It usually fails *loudly*: requests time out, errors spike, the on-call gets paged.

**Cost monitoring** asks whether you're bleeding money. LLM costs scale with tokens, not requests; one pathological query that triggers a 50k-token retrieval can blow a daily budget in an hour. It fails *expensively*: the CFO calls before the user does.

A mature monitoring setup has all three. Teams that ship only operational monitoring (the easiest pillar) are flying blind on quality and cost — the two pillars where AI behaves least like traditional software.

sections.title: 3. Drift Detection (Critical Section)
sections.body:
**Drift** is the slow change in the statistical properties of your inputs, outputs, or input→output relationship over time. It is the single most important failure mode in production AI, because it is invisible to operational metrics and silent to users until trust is gone.

### 3.1 Three types of drift

**Data drift (input drift).** The distribution of user queries changes. Example: a tax-prep chatbot trained on 2023 questions sees a flood of "2024 standard deduction" queries in January. The model still answers, but with 2023 numbers. Detection: compare the embedding distribution of today's queries to a stored baseline using cosine-distance histograms or PSI on binned embeddings.

**Concept drift.** The relationship between input and correct answer changes — the world moves, the model doesn't. Example: a model trained to recommend "stable" tech stocks recommends SVB in March 2023. The query ("best tech stocks") didn't change; the correct answer did. Detection: requires labeled feedback or outcome data; track accuracy on a rolling golden set.

**Prediction drift (output drift).** The distribution of model outputs changes, even if inputs didn't. Often caused by a silent model upgrade on the provider side, a prompt change, or a temperature tweak. Example: a support bot starts producing 30% longer answers overnight because someone bumped `max_tokens`. Detection: track length, sentiment, refusal rate, and LLM-judge score distributions over time.

### 3.2 Detection techniques

**Statistical tests** compare two distributions numerically. The big four:

- **KS test (Kolmogorov-Smirnov)** — maximum vertical distance between two CDFs. Sensitive to shape shifts; returns a p-value. Good for 1D continuous metrics (latency, faithfulness scores).
- **PSI (Population Stability Index)** — `Σ (p_i − q_i) · ln(p_i / q_i)` over binned counts. Industry favorite because it gives an interpretable magnitude: <0.1 stable, 0.1–0.25 watch, >0.25 drift. No p-value assumptions, works on any binned distribution.
- **KL divergence** — `Σ p_i · ln(p_i / q_i)`. Asymmetric; measures the information lost when q approximates p. Sensitive to zero bins.
- **JS divergence** — symmetric, smoothed version of KL. Always finite; bounded in [0, ln 2]. Easier to use, slightly less interpretable.

**Embedding-based drift** projects each input query (or output) into embedding space and compares the distribution of embeddings to a baseline. Cosine-distance histograms, average pairwise distance, or k-means cluster proportions all work. This catches semantic drift that tokens miss: "How do I cancel?" and "How do I terminate my subscription?" are different tokens but the same cluster.

**LLM-judge-based drift** samples N outputs per day, runs each through a judge LLM with a fixed rubric, and tracks the score distribution. Slow and not free, but the only method that directly measures *quality* drift rather than proxying it.

### 3.3 Code: computing PSI

```python
import numpy as np

def psi(baseline, current, bins=10, eps=1e-6):
    """Population Stability Index. <0.1 stable, >0.25 = drift."""
    edges = np.histogram_bin_edges(baseline, bins=bins)
    p, _ = np.histogram(baseline, bins=edges)
    q, _ = np.histogram(current,   bins=edges)
    p = np.clip(p / p.sum(), eps, None)
    q = np.clip(q / q.sum(), eps, None)
    return float(np.sum((p - q) * np.log(p / q)))

# baseline = faithfulness scores from launch week (n=1000)
# current  = faithfulness scores from this week's judge sample
score = psi(baseline, current)
# 0.04 -> stable, 0.18 -> investigate, 0.62 -> page
```

### 3.4 Comparison of drift detection methods

| Method | What it measures | Cost | Sensitivity | When to use |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| KS test | 1D distribution shift | Low | High (p-value) | Latency, faithfulness scores |
| PSI | Binned distribution shift | Low | Medium (magnitude) | Industry default; any metric |
| KL divergence | Information loss | Low | High, unstable on empty bins | Theoretical analysis |
| JS divergence | Symmetric KL | Low | Medium, always finite | Multi-distribution comparison |
| Embedding cosine drift | Semantic input shift | Medium (need embedder) | Catches token-invisible drift | Query/topic drift |
| LLM-judge sampling | Quality drift | High (judge calls) | Direct on quality | The ground truth check |

Rule of thumb: PSI on faithfulness scores + embedding drift on queries catches 80% of issues. LLM-judge sampling on 1% of traffic catches the rest.

sections.title: 4. Quality Monitoring in Production
sections.body:
Quality is the pillar that doesn't monitor itself. You cannot ask every production output "are you correct?" — there is no ground truth at request time. So you approximate.

**Continuous evaluation (offline sampling).** Sample N% of production traffic (typically 1–5%), persist inputs/outputs/context to an eval store, and run your eval suite offline against them. This is the workhorse: it turns production traffic into a continuously refreshing golden set. Score with reference-free metrics (faithfulness, groundedness, answer relevance) so you don't need labels.

**Implicit feedback.** Signals users give without rating: copy button, regenerate click, dwell time, follow-up clarifying question, edit-before-send. These are *noisy but plentiful*. A regenerate click is a strong negative signal; a copy is a weak positive.

**Explicit feedback.** Thumbs up/down, star ratings, "was this helpful?" Noisy in the opposite direction: biased, sparse, and skewed toward extreme experiences (happy users don't rate).

**LLM-as-judge on production samples.** Run a strong judge model on a 0.5% sample with a fixed rubric. Treat the judge score as a metric, track its distribution over time, and drift-test it with PSI. The judge is your scalable, always-on QA team.

**Hallucination rate tracking.** For RAG systems specifically, track the rolling 24h faithfulness distribution. A spike in low-faithfulness scores is the leading indicator of retrieval regression — usually a stale or corrupted index.

**Reference-free vs reference-based.** In production you almost never have the gold answer, so reference-free metrics (faithfulness to retrieved context, internal consistency, judge rubric) dominate. Reference-based metrics (exact match, F1, BERTScore) only apply to benchmark traffic or shadow-evaluated known queries.

```
                   PRODUCTION TRAFFIC
                          |
              +-----------+-----------+ sampled 1-5%
              |           |           |
           serve       log trace    sample -> eval store
              |           |           |
           user         full         reference-free
           feedback    context       metrics (faithfulness,
              |           |           groundedness, judge)
              |           |           |
              +-----+-----+-----------+
                    |
              quality dashboard
              (rolling 24h p50/p95,
               drift score, judge dist)
                    |
              drift detected? --> alert + add to golden set
                    |
              retrain/redeploy (file 10)
```

sections.title: 5. Operational Monitoring
sections.body:
This is the pillar that looks most like traditional observability — but with AI-specific shape.

**Latency.** Track p50, p95, and p99. For AI, **p99 matters most**: a single 30-second generation is more damaging than a 200ms median shift, because users interpret long latency as "the bot is thinking hard" and then as "it's broken." Also track **time-to-first-token (TTFT)** separately — for streaming, TTFT is the perceived latency; total time is back-end cost.

**Throughput.** Requests/sec is the wrong unit for AI. Use **tokens/sec** — a request that returns 2k tokens costs ten times the bandwidth of one returning 200. Token throughput is what your provider rate-limits and what your bills track.

**Error rates.** Decompose by type, because the fix is different for each: API errors (provider, retry), timeouts (load shedding), JSON parse failures (schema validation), refusals (safety policy), truncated outputs (raise `max_tokens`). Aggregate "error rate" hides actionable detail.

**Cache hit rate.** Two flavors: **prompt caching** (provider-side, prefix reuse) and **semantic caching** (your side, embedding-similarity match). Both reduce cost and latency; track hit rate, miss rate, and false-positive rate (semantic cache returning wrong-but-similar answer).

**Queue depth.** For agents and batch pipelines, queue depth is the early warning that throughput is saturating — before latency degrades.

**Tool/API failure rates.** For agents, a tool that starts failing 30% of the time will look like "agent accuracy dropped" if you don't break it out. Track per-tool success rate, latency, and timeout rate.

**Per-model breakdown.** If you route between models (cheap model for easy queries, expensive for hard), monitor each separately. A regression in the cheap model is invisible in aggregate.

| Metric | Healthy | Watch | Page |
|---|---|---|---|
| Latency p95 | < 2.0s | 2.0–4.0s | > 4.0s |
| Latency p99 | < 5.0s | 5.0–10.0s | > 10.0s |
| Time-to-first-token p95 | < 800ms | 800ms–1.5s | > 1.5s |
| Error rate (non-refusal) | < 0.5% | 0.5–2% | > 2% |
| Refusal rate | baseline ± 20% | ± 50% | > 2× baseline |
| Cache hit rate | > 30% | 10–30% | < 10% (if previously higher) |
| Tool failure rate (per tool) | < 1% | 1–5% | > 5% |
| Queue depth | 0 | 1–50 | > 50 sustained |

Thresholds are starting points, not laws. Set them from your own baseline; the table above is a calibration target.

sections.title: 6. Cost & Token Monitoring
sections.body:
LLM costs are the only metric that can surprise a CFO. A bug that doubles prompt length doubles the bill — invisibly, until the invoice arrives.

**Cost-per-request** is the basic metric. Track its distribution, not just the mean: a heavy-tailed distribution means a few pathological requests dominate spend.

**Cost-per-task-success** is the better metric. A model that costs 2× per request but succeeds 3× more often is cheaper *per successful outcome*. Tie cost to a quality signal; otherwise you'll optimize toward the cheapest, dumbest model.

**Token efficiency** = output tokens / input tokens. A RAG system with 8k-token contexts and 50-token answers has efficiency 1:160; that's not necessarily bad, but sudden drops (e.g., 1:40) usually mean retrieval is surfacing irrelevant context that the model has to wade through.

**Model mix tracking.** If you route between GPT-4o, Claude Haiku, and a local Llama, track share of traffic and share of cost per model. A routing bug that sends 80% to the expensive model is the most common silent cost regression.

**Budget alerts.** Set daily and monthly budgets at the *project* level, not the account level. Alert at 50%, 80%, 95%. Hard-stop at 100% if you can — a runaway loop can burn $10k in an afternoon.

**Anomaly detection on spend.** Cost is non-stationary (weekdays vs weekends, seasonal). Use a rolling 7-day same-hour baseline, alert when today's hour is > 3σ above the matched baseline.

sections.title: 7. Alerting Strategy
sections.body:
Bad alerting is worse than no alerting — it trains the on-call to ignore pages (alert fatigue) and masks real signals in noise.

**What to alert on.** Things that are (a) actionable, (b) time-sensitive, and (c) exceed a threshold you've validated. Faithfulness dropping 5% over a week is actionable. Latency p99 spiking to 12s is actionable. "Cost is up 3%" with no baseline is noise.

**What NOT to alert on.** Raw values without baselines. Single-request failures. Cosmetic metric changes. Anything you wouldn't wake someone up for.

**Severity levels.**

- **P0 — page on-call.** System is broken or about to break catastrophically. Quality below SLO, error rate > 5%, cost burn rate projected to exceed monthly budget in 24h.
- **P1 — Slack alert.** Investigate within business hours. Drift detected, latency p95 elevated, cache hit rate dropped 20%.
- **P2 — dashboard only.** Visible but no action needed yet. Watch trends.
- **P3 — log only.** For post-hoc analysis. Individual request failures, single-user anomalies.

**SLOs and SLIs for AI.** A **Service Level Indicator (SLI)** is the measurement; a **Service Level Objective (SLO)** is the target. AI SLOs are usually quality-bound, not just availability-bound:

- *SLI*: faithfulness score on sampled production traffic, 24h rolling.
- *SLO*: faithfulness ≥ 0.85 over rolling 24h, 99% of the time (error budget = 1%).
- *Alert*: page if rolling 24h faithfulness < 0.80 (SLO − budget).

| Condition | Severity | Action |
|---|---|---|
| Faithfulness 24h rolling < 0.80 | P0 | Page on-call; consider rollback |
| PSI on faithfulness > 0.25 | P1 | Slack #ai-alerts; investigate |
| Latency p99 > 10s for 5 min | P0 | Page on-call |
| Latency p95 > 4s for 10 min | P1 | Slack alert |
| Error rate > 5% for 2 min | P0 | Page on-call |
| Refusal rate > 2× baseline | P1 | Slack alert; check safety policy |
| Cache hit rate < 10% (was 30%) | P2 | Dashboard; investigate index |
| Daily cost > 1.5× 7d matched baseline | P1 | Slack #ai-cost |
| Monthly spend > 95% of budget | P0 | Page + auto-throttle |
| Single user > 10% of daily cost | P2 | Dashboard; possible abuse |

sections.title: 8. User Feedback Loops
sections.body:
Signals from users are the only ground truth you get at scale — but only if you capture and route them.

**Explicit feedback** (thumbs, stars, "report issue") is high-signal-per-click but sparse and biased. Users who rate are disproportionately either very happy or very angry; the silent majority in the middle is invisible.

**Implicit feedback** is denser and less biased:
- **Copy button** — positive signal; user found the answer useful enough to reuse.
- **Regenerate click** — strong negative; the first answer was bad enough to ask again.
- **Dwell time** on answer — bimodal: very short = dismissive; very long = either reading carefully or confused.
- **Follow-up clarification** ("no, I meant…") — negative signal on the prior turn.
- **Edit-before-send** on the *next* message — user is reformulating, prior turn was misunderstood.

**Bias: happy users don't rate.** A 4.8-star average can hide a 20% silent failure rate. Weight implicit signals more heavily; use explicit feedback for outlier detection, not averaging.

**Closing the loop.** Feedback only matters if it changes the system. The closed loop is: production feedback → labeled samples → golden dataset → eval run → regression detection → retraining/redeployment.

```
PRODUCTION
   |
   +-- thumbs / regenerate / copy / dwell  (signals)
   |          |
   |          v
   |   FEEDBACK QUEUE
   |          |   (filter: high-confidence negatives only)
   |          v
   |   HUMAN LABELING (triage, label, dedupe)
   |          |
   |          v
   |   GOLDEN DATASET (refreshed weekly)
   |          |
   |          v
   |   EVAL SUITE (run on every model/prompt change)
   |          |
   |          v
   |   DECISION: ship / hold / rollback
   |          |
   +----------+ (new model deployed; cycle repeats)
```

Without this loop, feedback buttons are theater. The single most important question to ask about your feedback system: *does a thumbs-down ever cause a code change?*

sections.title: 9. A/B Testing for AI Systems
sections.body:
A/B testing AI is harder than A/B testing traditional software for three reasons:

**Network effects.** A model learns from all traffic, not just its own arm. If you A/B test "model A" vs "model B" but both share a feedback database, B's wins may come from A's training data. The arms aren't independent.

**Long-tail tasks.** AI quality is dominated by the long tail. The head queries (80% of traffic) are easy and both models ace them. The tail (20% of traffic, 80% of the quality signal) needs weeks of traffic to reach statistical power. Naive 50/50 tests underpowered to detect 2% quality shifts need 100k+ samples per arm.

**Non-stationarity.** User behavior shifts mid-experiment. A/B test results from Monday don't generalize to Saturday.

**Interleaved testing.** Instead of serving model A to half the users and model B to the other half, interleave: for each user, randomly choose A or B per query. Faster signal (every user contributes to both arms), controls for user-level variance, and reaches significance in ~10× fewer queries.

**Guardrail metrics.** When optimizing for the primary metric (e.g., answer quality), watch the guardrails (latency, cost, refusal rate). An improvement that doubles cost or triples p99 latency is not a ship. Define guardrails *before* the experiment; rejecting on guardrail violation after the fact is p-hacking.

**Sample size.** For a 2-percentage-point quality shift with σ=0.15, you need roughly n = (2.8 × 0.15 / 0.02)² ≈ 440 samples per arm for 80% power. For rare-event metrics (hallucination rate at 1%), you need thousands. Use a power calculator before launching, not after.

sections.title: 10. Tools Landscape
sections.body:
| Tool | Strength | Drift? | Tracing? | OSS? | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Arize AI | Full AI observability; deep drift + eval | Yes | Yes | No | Commercial; enterprise-grade |
| Datadog LLM Monitoring | Integrated with existing Datadog stack | Yes | Yes | No | Best if already on Datadog |
| WhyLabs | Drift-first; embedding + data quality | Yes (flagship) | Partial | No | Strong on drift, lighter on traces |
| Langfuse | OSS monitoring + tracing + eval | Yes | Yes | Yes | Self-hostable; popular OSS pick |
| LangSmith | Tight LangChain integration; eval + monitor | Yes | Yes | No | Best if on LangChain stack |
| Helicone | Proxy-based; drop-in, captures everything | Yes | Yes | Yes (partial) | Sits in front of provider |
| Prometheus + Grafana | General metrics; fully custom | DIY | DIY | Yes | Free but you build AI layer yourself |
| New Relic AI Monitoring | APM-extended for AI | Yes | Yes | No | Best if already on New Relic |

Selection logic: already on Datadog/New Relic → use their AI module. OSS-required → Langfuse. Drift is the headline concern → WhyLabs. Tightly coupled to LangChain → LangSmith. Want zero code changes → Helicone proxy. Want full control → Prometheus + Grafana + custom.

sections.title: 12. Code Example
sections.body:
`/home/z/my-project/scripts/ai_monitoring.py` — pure Python (numpy + stdlib). Simulates a 2400-request stream, holds a 1000-request baseline, and detects faithfulness drift via PSI on a rolling window.

```python
"""Production AI monitoring: simulates a stream of production metrics
(latency, cost, faithfulness), detects faithfulness drift via Population
Stability Index (PSI), and fires alerts when PSI > threshold."""
import numpy as np
from collections import deque

ALERT_THRESHOLD = 0.2   # PSI > 0.1 = watch, > 0.2 = drift, > 0.5 = severe

def psi(baseline, current, bins=10, eps=1e-6):
    """Population Stability Index between two distributions.

    PSI = sum((p_i - q_i) * ln(p_i / q_i))  over histogram bins.
    Stable distributions score ~0; shifted distributions score >0.2.
    """
    edges = np.histogram_bin_edges(baseline, bins=bins)
    p, _ = np.histogram(baseline, bins=edges)
    q, _ = np.histogram(current, bins=edges)
    p = np.clip(p / max(p.sum(), 1), eps, None)
    q = np.clip(q / max(q.sum(), 1), eps, None)
    return float(np.sum((p - q) * np.log(p / q)))

def pct(samples, q):
    arr = list(samples) if not hasattr(samples, "__len__") else samples
    return float(np.quantile(arr, q)) if len(arr) else float("nan")

def simulate_request(rng, drift=False):
    """One production request: (latency_s, cost_usd, faithfulness in [0,1])."""
    latency = float(np.clip(rng.normal(0.85 if not drift else 1.45, 0.22), 0.1, 8.0))
    cost = float(np.clip(rng.normal(0.004, 0.001), 0, 0.05))
    a, b = (8.0, 2.2) if not drift else (2.5, 5.0)  # mean faith 0.78 -> 0.33
    faith = float(np.clip(rng.beta(a, b), 0, 1))
    return latency, cost, faith

def monitor(n=2400, window=500, drift_start=1200):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
    baseline = np.array([simulate_request(rng)[2] for _ in range(1000)])
    print(f"baseline faithfulness: mean={baseline.mean():.3f} "
          f"p5={pct(baseline, 0.05):.3f} p95={pct(baseline, 0.95):.3f}")
    fb = deque(maxlen=window); lat = deque(maxlen=window)
    cost = deque(maxlen=window); alerts, spend = [], 0.0
    for i in range(n):
        drift = i >= drift_start
        l, c, f = simulate_request(rng, drift=drift)
        fb.append(f); lat.append(l); cost.append(c); spend += c
        if i > 0 and i % window == 0 and len(fb) == window:
            score = psi(baseline, np.array(fb))
            status = "DRIFT-ALERT" if score > ALERT_THRESHOLD else "ok"
            print(f"[t={i:4d}] PSI={score:.3f} lat_p95={pct(lat, 0.95):.2f}s "
                  f"p99={pct(lat, 0.99):.2f}s spend=${spend:.2f} -> {status}")
            if score > ALERT_THRESHOLD and (not alerts or alerts[-1][0] != i):
                alerts.append((i, round(score, 3)))
    return alerts

if __name__ == "__main__":
    alerts = monitor()
    print(f"\nTotal drift alerts: {len(alerts)}; "
          f"first at t={alerts[0][0] if alerts else 'n/a'}")
```

Expected output (drift injected at t=1200; window=500; first drift check at t=1500):

```
baseline faithfulness: mean=0.787 p5=0.566 p95=0.950
[t= 500] PSI=0.061 lat_p95=1.22s p99=1.34s spend=$2.01 -> ok
[t=1000] PSI=0.028 lat_p95=1.22s p99=1.37s spend=$4.00 -> ok
[t=1500] PSI=1.121 lat_p95=1.79s p99=1.93s spend=$5.99 -> DRIFT-ALERT
[t=2000] PSI=10.057 lat_p95=1.83s p99=1.92s spend=$8.04 -> DRIFT-ALERT

Total drift alerts: 2; first at t=1500
```

The pre-drift windows score PSI ≈ 0.03–0.06 (stable). The first window that includes drifted traffic scores 1.12 — well past the 0.2 alert threshold. Latency also shifts (mean jumps from 0.85s to 1.45s in the simulator), which the p95/p99 columns capture. This is the minimum viable monitoring loop: baseline → rolling window → drift score → alert.

sections.title: 13. Common Pitfalls
sections.body:
- **Monitoring only ops, not quality.** Latency and error rate are green while faithfulness silently degrades. The dashboard lies by omission.
- **No baseline → can't detect drift.** PSI needs a stored reference distribution. Teams that skip baseline collection on day one cannot compute drift on day ninety.
- **Alerting on raw values instead of trends.** "Faithfulness is 0.87" is meaningless; "faithfulness dropped 0.07 in 48h" is actionable. Always diff against a baseline.
- **Ignoring the long tail.** Aggregate metrics hide catastrophic failure on the 1% of requests that matter most (high-value users, complex queries, edge-case tools).
- **No rollback plan when monitoring fires.** You detected the regression — now what? Without a one-click rollback to the prior model/prompt/index, detection is academic.
- **Cost as afterthought.** "We'll watch the bill at month-end" → surprise $40k invoice. Cost must be a first-class metric with daily budgets and per-user anomaly detection.
- **Alert fatigue.** Paging on every metric blip trains the on-call to ignore pages. Each alert must have a documented runbook; alerts without runbooks get demoted to P2.
- **Treating user feedback as ground truth.** Thumbs-up rate is biased, sparse, and lagging. Use it for outlier detection, not as your primary quality SLI.
- **Confusing provider-side metrics with your metrics.** Provider uptime is necessary but not sufficient; your prompts, retrieval, and tools all sit between the provider and your user.
- **Sampling bias in eval.** If you only sample "successful" requests into your eval store, you'll never measure failures. Sample by traffic, not by success.

quiz.explanation: A: Data (input) drift = query distribution shifts; detect via PSI or embedding-distance histograms on inputs. Concept drift = input→correct-answer relationship shifts; detect via rolling accuracy on a labeled golden set. Prediction (output) drift = output distribution shifts; detect via PSI on output length, faithfulness, or judge-score distributions.

quiz.question: Why is PSI often preferred over KL divergence for drift detection?
options: A: AI latency is heavy-tailed — long generations, multi-step agents, and tool calls can produce 10× median requests.

A: PSI is symmetric (KL is not), bounded-ish in interpretation (0.25 buckets), and stable on empty bins because of the epsilon-clip convention.
quiz.explanation: A: PSI is symmetric (KL is not), bounded-ish in interpretation (0.25 buckets), and stable on empty bins because of the epsilon-clip convention. KL diverges when a bin has zero count in either distribution. PSI also doesn't require distributional assumptions, which makes it usable on any binned metric.

A 200ms median improvement that hides a 30s p99 regression is a worse user experience, because users perceive "the bot froze" at the tail. p50 tracks efficiency; p99 tracks user-perceived reliability.
